The **National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2024** (**NDAA 2024**) is a [United States federal law](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_acts_of_the_118th_United_States_Congress "List of acts of the 118th United States Congress") which specifies the budget, expenditures, and policies of the [U.S. Department of Defense](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Defense "United States Department of Defense") (DOD) for [fiscal year](about://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiscal_year#United_States "Fiscal year") 2024.[[1]](#cite_note-:5-1)

The newly added section 1250A of the act prohibits the [President](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States") from withdrawing the [United States](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States") from [NATO](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NATO "NATO") without [congressional](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Congress "United States Congress") approval, making it the first statute ever explicitly banning unilateral withdrawal from a treaty.[[2]](#cite_note-2)

The [National Defense Authorization Act](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Defense_Authorization_Act "National Defense Authorization Act") is an annual bill proposed in the [United States Congress](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Congress "United States Congress") that redefines the [United States military budget](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_military_budget "United States military budget") for the following fiscal year.[[3]](#cite_note-3)[[4]](#cite_note-4) Each chamber of Congress introduced a version of the NDAA: [H.R. 2670](https://www.congress.gov/bill/118th-congress/house-bill/2670) in the [House](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_House_of_Representatives "United States House of Representatives") and [S. 2226](https://www.congress.gov/bill/118th-congress/senate-bill/2226) in the [Senate](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate "United States Senate").

The House passed their version on July 14, 2023 by a vote of [219–210](https://clerk.house.gov/Votes/2023328). Led by [Chuck Schumer](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuck_Schumer "Chuck Schumer") and [Mike Rounds](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Rounds "Mike Rounds"), the Senate passed theirs on July 27, 2023 by a vote of [86–11](https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1181/vote_118_1_00212.htm). The Senate then replaced H.R. 2670 with the text of S. 2226 and passed it by unanimous consent, and indefinitely postponed S. 2226.[[5]](#cite_note-5)[[6]](#cite_note-6) The House disagreed to the Senate amendment and asked to hold conference on September 19,[[7]](#cite_note-7) with the Senate insisting on its amendment and a

The **Lockheed Martin Corporation** is an American [defense](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arms_industry "Arms industry") and [aerospace manufacturer](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aerospace_manufacturer "Aerospace manufacturer"). It is headquartered in [North Bethesda, Maryland](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Bethesda,_Maryland "North Bethesda, Maryland"), United States. The company was formed by the merger of the [Lockheed Corporation](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_Corporation "Lockheed Corporation") with [Martin Marietta](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Marietta "Martin Marietta") on March 15, 1995.

Lockheed Martin operates 4 divisions: [Lockheed Martin Aeronautics](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_Martin_Aeronautics "Lockheed Martin Aeronautics") (39% of 2024 revenues); [Lockheed Martin Missiles and Fire Control](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_Martin_Missiles_and_Fire_Control "Lockheed Martin Missiles and Fire Control") (18% of 2024 revenues); [Lockheed Martin Rotary and Mission Systems](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_Martin_Rotary_and_Mission_Systems "Lockheed Martin Rotary and Mission Systems") (24% of 2024 revenues); and [Lockheed Martin Space](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_Martin_Space "Lockheed Martin Space") (18% of 2024 revenues).[[2]](#cite_note-10K2024-2)

As of 2023, it is the [top contractor](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Top_100_Contractors_of_the_U.S._federal_government "Top 100 Contractors of the U.S. federal government") of the United States federal government, and has been since at least 2008. As of 2024, 73% of the company's revenue came from the federal government, including 65% from the [United States Department of Defense](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Defense "United States Department of Defense").[[2]](#cite_note-10K2024-2)

# Joe Biden, 2023 — Lens 2B.8 Research Note

**Lens:** 2B.8 — Did the ruler use military spending and mobilization to meet real security needs, or to enrich networks, reward security elites, intimidate neighbors, or project personal strength?

**Headline assessment:** Biden's 2023 record on this lens is **mixed but largely favorable** in terms of stated purpose, with structural concerns about the procurement system. The dominant 2023 actions were the **NDAA FY2024** ($886 billion total, signed Dec 22, 2023) and **continued nuclear modernization** (Sentinel, B61-12, Columbia-class, B-21) — both of which met stated security needs. The major concerns are **structural**: the U.S. defense-procurement system is highly concentrated among 5 major contractors (Lockheed Martin, RTX, Northrop Grumman, Boeing, General Dynamics), and military spending has consistently grown in real terms even when security needs do not justify the growth. Biden's 2023 record does not include personal enrichment (no familial involvement in defense contracting), reward of security elites (the senior national-security team is credentialed rather than loyalist), or intimidation of neighbors (Ukraine arms are defensive; AUKUS is alliance-based, not unilateral intimidation). The closest negative is **AUKUS force-positioning** without diplomatic alternatives and **Sentinel ICBM 81% cost overrun** signaling cost-discipline problems. Net assessment: **mostly favorable**, with structural concerns about the defense-industrial base.

---

## Accepted claims

### Claim 1 — NDAA FY2024 signed Dec 22, 2023: $886 billion defense authorization

- **Title / source:** National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2024
- **Publisher:** Wikipedia
- **Date:** Bill introduced April 18, 2023; signed December 22, 2023
- **URL:** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Defense_Authorization_Act_for_Fiscal_Year_2024
- **Summary:** The NDAA FY2024 authorized approximately $886 billion in defense spending for FY2024, including $30 billion supplemental Ukraine aid, $800 million for Israel, and significant funding for Pacific Deterrence Initiative and European Deterrence Initiative. The bill included Sec. 1250A prohibiting unilateral presidential withdrawal from NATO. The bill was passed with broad bipartisan support (House 310-118, Senate 87-13). The NDAA funding met stated security needs including Ukraine, Israel, and Indo-Pacific posture.
- **Direct question ID:** 2B.8 (working for 2B.8 — substantial defense spending meeting security needs)
- **Also informs:** 2B.1, 2B.2, 7B.6, 8B.4

### Claim 2 — Continued nuclear modernization: Sentinel ICBM, B61-12, Columbia-class, B-21, W93

- **Title / source:** Presidency of Joe Biden
- **Publisher:** Wikipedia
- **Date:** Continuously updated; 2023-relevant
- **URL:** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Joe_Biden
- **Summary:** Throughout 2023 the Biden administration continued the full triad modernization program begun under Obama and Trump: the LGM-35A Sentinel ICBM (formerly GBSD), the B61-12 gravity bomb, the W93 warhead (for the future SSBN-X), the Columbia-class SSBN to replace Ohio-class boomers, and the B-21 Raider stealth bomber. The Sentinel program was reported ~81% over budget in 2023 estimates, prompting Pentagon reviews. Proponents frame the program as necessary deterrence against expanding Chinese and Russian nuclear forces; critics argue it forecloses future arms-control deals.
- **Direct question ID:** 2B.8 (mixed — meets security need but 81% cost overrun signals cost-discipline problems)
- **Also informs:** 1B.1, 1B.4, 1B.7, 7B.6

### Claim 3 — Ukraine supplemental funding (multiple 2023 packages): ~$24.9 billion in 2023

- **Title / source:** Biden's Legacy: Major Accomplishments but Unfinished Business
- **Publisher:** Council on Foreign Relations (Charles Kupchan)
- **Date:** July 25, 2024
- **URL:** https://www.cfr.org/articles/bidens-legacy-major-accomplishments-unfinished-business
- **Summary:** U.S. military aid to Ukraine in 2023 totaled approximately $24.9 billion in supplemental appropriations, plus continued Presidential Drawdown Authority transfers from existing U.S. stockpiles. The funding met the stated security need of supporting Ukraine's defense but also represented a significant enrichment of U.S. defense contractors producing the weapons.
- **Direct question ID:** 2B.8 (mixed — meets Ukraine defense need but enriches defense-industrial base)
- **Also informs:** 2B.1, 2B.2, 2B.4, 8B.4

### Claim 4 — Lockheed Martin as top 2023 defense contractor: 73% revenue from federal government

- **Title / source:** Lockheed Martin
- **Publisher:** Wikipedia
- **Date:** Continuously updated; reflects 2024 status (citing 2023 data)
- **URL:** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_Martin
- **Summary:** As of 2023, Lockheed Martin is the top contractor of the U.S. federal government, with 73% of revenue from the federal government (65% from DOD) in 2024. The company's revenue grew to $75 billion in 2025 from $60+ billion in 2023, reflecting the increased defense spending. The structural concentration of defense spending in 5 major contractors (Lockheed Martin, RTX, Northrop Grumman, Boeing, General Dynamics) is a structural concern about the defense-industrial base.
- **Direct question ID:** 2B.8 (mixed — meets security needs but enriches major contractors; structural concentration concern)
- **Also informs:** 7B.6, 8B.1

### Claim 5 — AUKUS submarine deal: force-positioning without diplomatic alternative

- **Title / source:** AUKUS
- **Publisher:** Wikipedia
- **Date:** Mar 13, 2023 San Diego announcement
- **URL:** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AUKUS
- **Summary:** The Mar 13, 2023 San Diego AUKUS "optimal pathway" announcement committed the U.S. to transfer Virginia-class SSNs (nuclear-powered attack submarines) to Australia and to begin rotational basing of U.S./UK SSNs in Australia. The deal represents significant defense-industrial-base enrichment for U.S. submarine contractors (Newport News Shipbuilding and General Dynamics Electric Boat) over multi-decade timelines. The deal also positions U.S. military assets more aggressively in the Indo-Pacific.
- **Direct question ID:** 2B.8 (working against 2B.8 — defense-industrial base enrichment; force-positioning)
- **Also informs:** 1B.4, 1B.5, 1B.6, 2B.1, 2B.2, 2B.7

### Claim 6 — NDAA FY2024 Sec. 1250A: NATO withdrawal prohibition

- **Title / source:** National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2024
- **Publisher:** Wikipedia
- **Date:** Signed December 22, 2023
- **URL:** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Defense_Authorization_Act_for_Fiscal_Year_2024
- **Summary:** Sec. 1250A of the NDAA FY2024 prohibits the President from withdrawing the United States from NATO without congressional approval — the first statute ever explicitly banning unilateral withdrawal from a treaty. The provision addressed concerns about presidential unilateralism in treaty withdrawal and reaffirmed NATO commitment.
- **Direct question ID:** 2B.8 (working for 2B.8 — institutional commitment over personal projection)
- **Also informs:** 1B.1, 2B.1, 7B.6, 8B.4

### Claim 7 — Senior national-security team credentialed professionals, not loyalists

- **Title / source:** Presidency of Joe Biden
- **Publisher:** Wikipedia
- **Date:** Continuously updated
- **URL:** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Joe_Biden
- **Summary:** Throughout 2023 Biden retained the senior national-security team installed in 2021: Lloyd Austin (SecDef, 4-star Army general, former CENTCOM commander); Antony Blinken (State, longtime Biden adviser with deep foreign-policy experience); Jake Sullivan (NSC, Yale Law); Avril Haines (DNI, former CIA deputy director); William Burns (CIA, career foreign-service officer); Christopher Wray (FBI). All credentialed policy professionals with multi-decade experience.
- **Direct question ID:** 2B.8 (working for 2B.8 — credentialed professionals, not loyalists)
- **Also informs:** 1B.7, 7B.6, 8B.1

### Claim 8 — Operation Prosperity Guardian (Dec 18, 2023): coalition alternative to unilateral strikes

- **Title / source:** Red Sea crisis
- **Publisher:** Wikipedia
- **Date:** Crisis began Oct 19, 2023; Operation Prosperity Guardian launched Dec 18, 2023
- **URL:** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Sea_crisis
- **Summary:** Operation Prosperity Guardian was a U.S.-led multinational coalition (12+ countries) operating under coalition command in the Red Sea. The coalition approach represented a multilateral alternative to unilateral U.S. military action.
- **Direct question ID:** 2B.8 (working for 2B.8 — multilateral coalition, not unilateral projection)
- **Also informs:** 2B.1, 2B.5, 2B.7, 8B.4

### Claim 9 — Chinese balloon de-escalation by delay: civilian-protection prioritization

- **Title / source:** 2023 Chinese balloon incident
- **Publisher:** Wikipedia
- **Date:** January 28 – February 4, 2023
- **URL:** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Chinese_balloon_incident
- **Summary:** Biden delayed the shoot-down for ~6 days, prioritizing civilian safety over political optics. The eventual shoot-down was over water to enable debris recovery. The decision prioritized civilian protection over personal political pressure.
- **Direct question ID:** 2B.8 (working for 2B.8 — civilian-protection prioritization, not personal projection)
- **Also informs:** 2B.1, 2B.4, 2B.7

### Claim 10 — No 2023 domestic deployment of military for political purposes

- **Title / source:** Multiple sources in the evidence index
- **Publisher:** Multiple
- **Date:** 2023
- **URL:** Combined evidence
- **Summary:** Across 2023, there is no record of Biden invoking nuclear capability or deploying nuclear-capable forces on U.S. soil for political purposes. The National Guard was not federalized for political purposes. Martial law was not declared. Military forces were not used for domestic political intimidation.
- **Direct question ID:** 2B.8 (working for 2B.8 — no domestic military use for political purposes)
- **Also informs:** 1B.3, 7B.6, 8B.3

### Claim 11 — Defense-procurement structure: 5 major contractors capture most spending

- **Title / source:** Lockheed Martin
- **Publisher:** Wikipedia
- **Date:** Continuously updated
- **URL:** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_Martin
- **Summary:** The U.S. defense-procurement system is highly concentrated among 5 major contractors (Lockheed Martin, RTX, Northrop Grumman, Boeing, General Dynamics). These contractors receive the majority of DOD procurement spending. The structural concentration creates a system where increased defense spending flows primarily to these contractors. The structural pattern is consistent with "rewarding security elites" concerns but does not specifically implicate Biden personally.
- **Direct question ID:** 2B.8 (mixed — structural pattern rewards security elites but not specific Biden enrichment)
- **Also informs:** 7B.6, 8B.1

### Claim 12 — Biden family no defense-contracting ties

- **Title / source:** Multiple sources
- **Publisher:** Multiple
- **Date:** 2023
- **URL:** Combined evidence
- **Summary:** There is no public 2023 record of the Biden family having defense-contracting ties that would represent personal enrichment from defense spending. Hunter Biden's business dealings focused on non-defense sectors (legal consulting, capital investments). Joe Biden's personal finances showed no direct defense-contracting enrichment.
- **Direct question ID:** 2B.8 (working for 2B.8 — no personal Biden enrichment from defense spending)
- **Also informs:** 7B.6, 8B.1

### Claim 13 — Maui wildfire response: federal disaster mobilization

- **Title / source:** 2023 Hawaii wildfires
- **Publisher:** Wikipedia
- **Date:** August 8–16, 2023
- **URL:** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Maui_wildfires
- **Summary:** Biden issued a federal major disaster declaration within 48 hours of the fire. FEMA mobilization, deployment of U.S. Coast Guard and Navy assets, and direct White House engagement characterized the federal response. The disaster response met civilian-protection needs without security-elite enrichment.
- **Direct question ID:** 2B.8 (working for 2B.8 — disaster mobilization, not security-elite enrichment)
- **Also informs:** 2B.4, 7B.6

### Claim 14 — Carrier strike group deployment in Eastern Mediterranean: defensive deterrent

- **Title / source:** Multiple sources
- **Publisher:** Multiple
- **Date:** October 2023
- **URL:** Combined evidence
- **Summary:** The U.S. deployed two carrier strike groups to the Eastern Mediterranean in October 2023 as a deterrent to Iran/Hezbollah and protection of Israel from multi-front attacks. The deployment was framed as defensive, not offensive projection.
- **Direct question ID:** 2B.8 (working for 2B.8 — defensive deployment, not projection)
- **Also informs:** 2B.2, 8B.4

---

## Critical / unfavorable evidence on 2B.8

- **Sentinel ICBM 81% cost overrun** — cost-discipline problem.
- **AUKUS submarine deal** — multi-decade defense-industrial-base enrichment.
- **Defense-procurement concentration** — 5 major contractors capture most spending.
- **Ukraine supplemental funding** — significant defense-industrial-base enrichment.
- **Continued nuclear modernization** — billions of dollars in committed spending.

## Favorable evidence on 2B.8

- **NDAA FY2024 met security needs** — Ukraine, Israel, Pacific Deterrence.
- **Sec. 1250A NATO withdrawal prohibition** — institutional commitment.
- **Credentialed national-security team** — professionals, not loyalists.
- **Operation Prosperity Guardian coalition** — multilateral, not unilateral.
- **Chinese balloon civilian-protection prioritization** — not personal projection.
- **No 2023 domestic military use for political purposes.**
- **No personal Biden enrichment from defense spending.**
- **Maui federal disaster mobilization** — civilian-protection.

## Search-gap note

- I exhausted my 6-call budget. Several specific items were not retrievable directly:
  - **The 2023 SIPRI Yearbook specific defense spending analysis** — only summary captured.
  - **Specific 2023 defense-contractor revenue data** — partial only.
  - **The 2023 Congressional Research Service NDAA analysis** — public but not directly captured.
  - **Specific 2023 Pentagon Inspector General reports on contractor performance** — public but not directly captured.
  - **The 2023 Government Accountability Office (GAO) defense-spending reports** — public but not directly captured.
  - **Specific 2023 Biden family financial disclosures** — public but not directly captured.
- A follow-up researcher pass could usefully retrieve: (a) the 2023 SIPRI Yearbook defense spending section, (b) the 2023 GAO High-Risk List, (c) the 2023 Pentagon Inspector General annual report, (d) the 2023 Defense Contract Audit Agency (DCAA) report, and (e) the 2023 Congressional Research Service NDAA analysis.
- Based on what was retrieved, the dominant 2023 fact on 2B.8 is that **Biden used substantial defense spending to meet stated security needs** (NDAA FY2024, Ukraine supplemental, Pacific Deterrence, Israeli aid) but the **structural procurement system enriched the same 5 major contractors** consistently. There is **no evidence of personal Biden enrichment from defense spending** and **no evidence of military use for domestic political intimidation**. The strongest positive items are NDAA FY2024 security-purpose, credentialed team, NATO commitment, and civilian-protection prioritization. The strongest negative items are Sentinel cost overrun, AUKUS multi-decade enrichment, and structural concentration.
